strengths: Clear problem motivation with convincing empirical evidence (Figure 1) that fixed caching schedules fail to adapt to rollout dynamics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 9 tasks with two dataset variants and 7 strong baselines, including real-world validation
Technically sound approach with well-justified design choices (sinusoidal embeddings, transformer encoder) validated through ablations
Achieves substantial practical speedups (3.6-4×) with 90%+ pruning while maintaining or improving task performance
Excellent efficiency of the pruner (<0.3% overhead) making the approach practical for real-time deployment
Thorough ablation studies (Table 4) demonstrating necessity of each component (pruner, reusing strategy, global loss)
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and well-written algorithms
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: observation-conditioned pruning is an incremental extension of prior learned pruning work; one-for-all reusing is a straightforward application of known cross-block redundancy; global sparsity loss is a reasonable but not novel design choice
Insufficient real-world validation: only one task (pick-and-release) with modest results (54% success, 45.1 Hz); claims of practical significance not fully supported by diverse real-world evidence
Unjustified critical hyperparameters: reference dataset size (5% with no ablation), target pruning rate ρ=91% (fixed across diverse tasks); no sensitivity analysis on these design choices
Incomplete failure analysis: Transport+Tool task drops to 50% success with no explanation; missing characterization of task properties that determine suitability for aggressive pruning

Global sparsity loss may impose suboptimal patterns: hard constraint (Eq. 10) enforces uniform pruning rate across rollout, potentially conflicting with optimal adaptive allocation; no discussion of this tradeoff
Reproducibility gaps: pruner training cost not reported, visual encoder architecture incomplete, per-task training overhead not discussed, code only mentioned via 'project page'
Technical details under-analyzed: STE bias for argmax not discussed, cached activation approximation error not quantified, generalization to out-of-distribution observations unclear

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling empirical evidence (leave-one-out analysis showing fixed schedules are suboptimal) that clearly establishes the need for rollout-adaptive pruning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 9 simulation task variants, real-world validation on Franka robot, and meaningful baseline comparisons including distillation methods

Technically sound methodology with proper use of STE for gradient flow, well-formulated optimization objective balancing fidelity and sparsity constraints, and a global sparsity loss that enables non-uniform resource allocation
Substantial practical improvements: 3.6-4× speedup while maintaining ~87% average success rate and >90% pruning ratio, addressing a real bottleneck for real-time robotic control

Thorough ablation studies demonstrating each component's contribution (Table 6 shows 37% performance drop without global sparsity loss), sensitivity analysis across pruning rates, and honest discussion of limitations and failure modes
Strong real-world results including counter-intuitive improvements on challenging tasks (Assembly Line: 26%→58% success with 44.3 Hz frequency) demonstrating practical value
Reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, public checkpoints, architecture diagrams, training curves, and reference to available datasets
weaknesses: Limited architectural scope: only evaluated on DP-T (transformer-based diffusion policy) with no assessment of generalization to other policy architectures or larger models; unclear applicability beyond current setting

Insufficient quantification of pruner overhead: claims 'negligible' computational cost but provides no actual latency measurements for pruner inference; actual speedup validity depends on this unquantified component

Critical gap in cross-task generalization analysis: no evaluation of whether pruners trained on one task transfer to others; unclear if method requires task-specific retraining, limiting practical applicability
Data efficiency of pruner training unexplored: pruner trained on only 5% of data with no systematic study of this trade-off or comparison with other data-efficient training strategies

Incomplete technical justifications: choice of 91% pruning rate appears purely empirical; no ablation on pruner architecture (3-layer MLP depth, transformer encoder necessity); why concatenate vs. sum sinusoidal embeddings lacks justification
Limited real-world validation scope: only 3 tasks with 20 trials each; real-world success rates substantially lower than simulation (78% vs. 100%+ on Lift) raising sim-to-real transfer concerns

Presentation clarity issues: heavy mathematical notation reduces readability; pruner architecture design decisions (especially sinusoidal encoding) explained only in appendix despite being critical; relationship between training and inference with one-for-all reusing unclear

Narrow comparison with distillation-based acceleration: Consistency Policy achieves 15× speedup but comparison relies on compute-matched analysis in appendix rather than clear guidance on method selection; main results don't establish when SAG is preferable

Missing ablations and analyses: no ablation on pruner architectural components; no analysis of pruning rate stability implications for safety-critical applications (±1.6% deviation observed); limited exploration of failure modes beyond observation robustness
